Unit 20 used logistic regression for *inference*: what does a change in X do to the
probability of the outcome? This tutorial uses the same model for *prediction*.
Once a model produces a probability for every case, someone has to decide which
cases to call "yes", and that decision has its own vocabulary and its own
mistakes. The example comes from data-quality work, deciding automatically what
kind of information each column of a spreadsheet holds, using a column-level
feature dataset built for the
[formex](https://lecy.github.io/formex/articles/feature-dataset.html) R package.
The steps are:

1. fit a logistic regression with `glm()`,
2. turn predicted probabilities into class predictions with a cutoff of 0.5,
3. build a confusion matrix,
4. read the model's performance through several accuracy metrics, and
5. move the cutoff --- including how to pick it when a false positive and a false
   negative do not cost the same.

We fit two models on the same data. The first is a **strong model**: it is right
about almost everything it flags and finds most of what it is looking for. The
second is a **lopsided model**: it is excellent at saying "no" and poor at saying
"yes", and the headline accuracy number hides that completely. The second model is
the one a threshold can fix.

## The data

Each row of the dataset is one *column* of a real table, described by numbers
computed from its values by formex's `fx_extract_features()`. The full dataset has
477 features; the teaching extract keeps a dozen interpretable ones plus the labels.
You don't need the formex package to follow along: the code below uses only base R,
and the data file loads straight from the course site.

```{r data}
path <- "data/type_features_logit.rds"   # the copy next to this file
if (!file.exists(path)) {
  path <- url("https://github.com/lecy/econometrics/raw/main/lectures4/classifiers/data/type_features_logit.rds")
}
d <- readRDS(path)
dim(d)
```

A few rows, showing the example values and some of the features:

```{r peek}
d[c(1, 2000, 4000), c("sample_values", "data_type", "semantic_type",
                      "n_digits_mean", "pct_all_digits", "unique_ratio")]
```

The features we use (all computed from the values alone --- the column header
never enters):

| Feature | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `n_digits_mean` | Average number of digits in the integer part of numeric values. |
| `log10_range` | Spread of numeric values, $\log_{10}$ of (max − min) relative to the scale of the values. |
| `pct_all_digits` | Share of values made entirely of digits. |
| `dig_entropy` | How evenly the digits 0--9 are used. Codes and serial numbers use all ten digits evenly; counts and prices do not. |
| `unique_ratio` | Distinct values / total values. Identifiers are (nearly) all unique. |
| `pct_chr_digit` | Share of characters that are digits. |
| `len_mean` | Average string length. |
| `pct_alnum_mixed` | Share of values mixing letters and digits (e.g. `089608776X`). |
| `lcp_frac` | Length of the prefix all values share, relative to value length (e.g. every value starts with `isbn `). |

Missing feature values (a numeric statistic on a text column, for instance) were
already imputed in the extract, following the per-feature rules described in the
[feature dataset guide](https://lecy.github.io/formex/articles/feature-dataset.html).

### Two binary outcomes

We create two yes/no outcomes:

- **`is_year`** --- is the column a calendar year (`1995, 2003, 2011, ...`)?
- **`is_id`** --- is the column an identifier (ISBNs, record IDs, DOIs, hashes)?

```{r outcomes}
d$is_year <- as.integer(d$semantic_type %in% "year")
d$is_id   <- as.integer(d$data_type == "identifier")

c(years = sum(d$is_year), ids = sum(d$is_id), all_columns = nrow(d))
round(100 * c(year = mean(d$is_year), id = mean(d$is_id)), 1)   # base rates, %
```

Both outcomes are **rare**: under 3% of columns. Rarity is the normal situation in
classification work (fraud, disease, defaults, and here, column types), and it is
exactly what makes plain "accuracy" misleading, as we will see.

### Train / test split

We fit each model on 70% of the rows and judge it on the 30% it never saw. Judging
a model on its own training data rewards memorization.

```{r split}
set.seed(2026)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(d), size = round(0.7 * nrow(d)))
train <- d[ train_rows, ]
test  <- d[-train_rows, ]
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
c(years_in_test = sum(test$is_year), ids_in_test = sum(test$is_id))
```

### A small toolkit

Two helper functions do the bookkeeping for the rest of the tutorial. The first
cross-tabulates truth against prediction; the second computes the metrics from the
four cells of that table.

```{r helpers}
confusion <- function(actual, predicted) {
  table(Actual    = factor(actual,    levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")),
        Predicted = factor(predicted, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")))
}

metrics <- function(actual, predicted) {
  TP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
  FP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
  FN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)
  TN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
  sens <- TP / (TP + FN)
  spec <- TN / (TN + FP)
  prec <- if (TP + FP > 0) TP / (TP + FP) else NA
  c(TP = TP, FP = FP, FN = FN, TN = TN,
    accuracy          = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN),
    no_info_rate      = max(mean(actual), 1 - mean(actual)),
    sensitivity       = sens,                  # a.k.a. recall, true positive rate
    specificity       = spec,                  # true negative rate
    precision         = prec,                  # a.k.a. positive predictive value
    npv               = TN / (TN + FN),        # negative predictive value
    F1                = 2 * TP / (2 * TP + FP + FN),
    balanced_accuracy = (sens + spec) / 2)
}
```

The confusion matrix is laid out with the positive class ("Yes") first:

|               | Predicted Yes       | Predicted No        |
|---------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Actual Yes** | TP (true positive)  | FN (false negative) |
| **Actual No**  | FP (false positive) | TN (true negative)  |

Every metric is a ratio of these four counts --- they differ only in *which* cells
they put in the numerator and denominator, which is to say which question they
answer:

| Metric | Formula | Question it answers |
|--------|---------|---------------------|
| Accuracy | (TP+TN) / all | What share of all calls were right? |
| Sensitivity (recall) | TP / (TP+FN) | Of the real positives, how many did we catch? |
| Specificity | TN / (TN+FP) | Of the real negatives, how many did we correctly leave alone? |
| Precision (PPV) | TP / (TP+FP) | When the model says "yes", how often is it right? |
| NPV | TN / (TN+FN) | When the model says "no", how often is it right? |
| F1 | 2TP / (2TP+FP+FN) | Harmonic mean of precision and recall; ignores TN. |
| Balanced accuracy | (sens+spec) / 2 | Accuracy with both classes weighted equally. |
| No-information rate | share of the majority class | The accuracy of always guessing the most common class. |

## Model 1: is this column a year?

A year column has a distinctive numeric fingerprint: the values are all digits,
they have four digits, and they sit in a narrow band (1900--2030), so their range
is small relative to their size. A linear term in `n_digits_mean` can't express
"close to 4" (both 2-digit and 9-digit columns are *not* years), so we build one
feature that measures the distance from four digits.

```{r year-feature}
train$digits_from_4 <- abs(train$n_digits_mean - 4)
test$digits_from_4  <- abs(test$n_digits_mean  - 4)
```

### Fit the model

```{r m-year}
m_year <- glm(is_year ~ digits_from_4 + log10_range + pct_all_digits,
              data = train, family = binomial)
summary(m_year)
```

The warning `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred` is not an error. It
means some training columns are so clearly *not* years (text columns, nine-digit
numbers) that the model gives them a probability indistinguishable from 0. That is
common when a class is well separated, and it is a hint that this model will
perform well.

Coefficients are on the **log-odds** scale. Exponentiating gives **odds ratios**,
which are easier to talk about:

```{r m-year-or}
round(exp(coef(m_year)), 4)
```

- `digits_from_4`: each extra digit away from four multiplies the odds of "year"
  by about `r f2(exp(coef(m_year))[["digits_from_4"]])` --- the odds
  collapse. This is the workhorse feature.
- `log10_range`: a wider spread of values sharply lowers the odds. Years cluster
  within a few decades.
- `pct_all_digits` is **not significant** and its sign is even slightly negative.
  That surprises people: aren't years all digits? They are --- but so are the
  many non-year numeric columns. Once we already know a column has four-digit
  numbers in a narrow range, *also* knowing that its values are all digits adds
  nothing. Logistic coefficients are always read **holding the other features
  constant**.

### Predict with a 0.5 cutoff

`predict(..., type = "response")` returns the model's estimated probability that
each test column is a year. The default decision rule calls it a year when that
probability exceeds 0.5.

```{r p-year}
test$p_year    <- predict(m_year, newdata = test, type = "response")
test$yhat_year <- as.integer(test$p_year > 0.5)

summary(test$p_year)
```

### Confusion matrix and metrics

```{r cm-year}
confusion(test$is_year, test$yhat_year)
met_year <- metrics(test$is_year, test$yhat_year)
round(met_year, 3)
```

```{r year-numbers, include = FALSE}
my <- met_year
```

How to read this:

- **Precision is high: `r f2(my["precision"])`.** When the model says a
  column is a year, it is wrong only `r my["FP"]` time(s) out of
  `r my["TP"] + my["FP"]`. A user acting on its "yes" calls can trust them.
- **Sensitivity is good but not perfect: `r f2(my["sensitivity"])`.** It
  finds `r my["TP"]` of the `r my["TP"] + my["FN"]` year columns in the test set
  and misses `r my["FN"]`.
- **Specificity and NPV are near 1.** With only
  `r sum(test$is_year)` years among `r nrow(test)` test columns, almost every
  column is a correct "no".
- **Accuracy is `r f3(my["accuracy"])`** --- but the no-information rate is
  `r f3(my["no_info_rate"])`: a "model" that always answers "not a year"
  would score nearly as well. For a rare outcome, accuracy says very little; F1
  (`r f2(my["F1"])`) and balanced accuracy (`r f2(my["balanced_accuracy"])`)
  are more informative because they don't let the sea of true negatives dominate.

It is worth looking at the mistakes. The misses are columns *labeled* "year" whose
values are not plain four-digit years: class-year codes (`Fr, Sr`), spelled
numbers, full dates, academic years (`2003/04`), Minguo-calendar years, and a
couple of plain labeling errors (a list of countries, a list of names). A model of
four-digit numbers *cannot* catch these --- and some of them it *should not*. The
false positives are columns of four-digit numbers in a narrow range that happen to
be ranks or codes: honest mistakes that look exactly like years.

```{r year-errors}
fn <- test$is_year == 1 & test$yhat_year == 0
fp <- test$is_year == 0 & test$yhat_year == 1
test[fn, c("sample_values", "p_year")]
test[fp, c("sample_values", "semantic_type", "p_year")]
```

This is a **strong, balanced model**: high precision, high sensitivity. Moving the
threshold would only trade a few misses for a few false alarms; there is not much
to gain.

## Model 2: is this column an identifier?

Identifiers are (nearly) all unique, use every digit evenly, often mix letters and
digits, often share a prefix, and tend to be long.

```{r m-id}
m_id <- glm(is_id ~ dig_entropy + unique_ratio + pct_chr_digit + len_mean +
              pct_alnum_mixed + lcp_frac,
            data = train, family = binomial)
signif(cbind(coef = coef(m_id), odds_ratio = exp(coef(m_id)),
             p_value = summary(m_id)$coefficients[, 4]), 3)
```

Digit entropy, digit share, mixed letters-and-digits, and a shared prefix all
raise the odds strongly. `unique_ratio` and `len_mean` add little once the others
are in the model (large p-values); we keep them to show that a non-significant
coefficient is not a reason the model fails, it is just a feature that the others
make redundant.

### Predict, cross-tabulate, measure

```{r cm-id}
test$p_id    <- predict(m_id, newdata = test, type = "response")
test$yhat_id <- as.integer(test$p_id > 0.5)

confusion(test$is_id, test$yhat_id)
met_id <- metrics(test$is_id, test$yhat_id)
round(met_id, 3)
```

```{r id-numbers, include = FALSE}
mi <- met_id
```

At a glance this model also looks excellent: **accuracy
`r f3(mi["accuracy"])`**, specificity `r f3(mi["specificity"])`,
precision `r f2(mi["precision"])`. But look at the first row of the matrix, the
actual identifiers:

- **Sensitivity is only `r f2(mi["sensitivity"])`.** Of the
  `r mi["TP"] + mi["FN"]` identifier columns in the test set the model catches
  `r mi["TP"]` and **misses `r mi["FN"]`**. It finds fewer than half of them.
- **Accuracy hides this entirely.** The no-information rate is
  `r f3(mi["no_info_rate"])` --- always answering "not an ID" scores
  `r round(100 * mi["no_info_rate"], 1)`%, and the model beats that by barely a
  point.
- **Balanced accuracy (`r f2(mi["balanced_accuracy"])`) and F1
  (`r f2(mi["F1"])`)** expose the problem: one class is handled
  near-perfectly, the other poorly.

This is the **lopsided** pattern: high specificity, low sensitivity. The model is
conservative --- it only says "yes" when it is very sure, so its "yes" calls are
usually right (decent precision) but it says "yes" too rarely.

> **A note on the word "precision".** In everyday speech "a precise model" means a
> good one. In classification, *precision* is one specific metric, TP / (TP + FP).
> Notice that the lopsided model's *precision* is fairly high --- the problem is
> its *sensitivity*. A model that is conservative on a rare class almost always
> looks like this: high specificity, high precision, low recall. Always report
> sensitivity and precision together.

### Why it happens: the rare class and the 0.5 cutoff

Logistic regression estimates probabilities that are, on average, faithful to the
data. When only `r round(100 * mean(train$is_id), 1)`% of training columns are
identifiers, the model's probabilities for real identifiers are pulled toward that
low base rate --- many land at 0.2 or 0.3, well above what non-IDs get, but below 0.5.

```{r id-hist, fig.height = 4.6}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4.5, 4, 2, 1))
brks <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.025)
hist(test$p_id[test$is_id == 0], breaks = brks, col = "gray75", border = "white",
     main = "Not an identifier", xlab = "", ylab = "columns")
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
hist(test$p_id[test$is_id == 1], breaks = brks, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "Identifier", xlab = "predicted probability of 'identifier'",
     ylab = "columns")
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
par(op)
```

The non-identifiers pile up near zero. The identifiers are spread out: the model
never gets very confident about any of them (the highest scores are around
`r f2(max(test$p_id[test$is_id == 1]))`), and more than half of them fall to the *left* of the red cutoff, many well above
zero. The model is **ranking** the columns well (identifiers get higher scores
than non-identifiers); the cutoff is just in the wrong place for this base rate.

The area under the ROC curve (AUC) measures ranking quality independent of any
cutoff: it is the probability that a randomly chosen identifier scores higher than
a randomly chosen non-identifier.

```{r auc}
auc <- function(actual, score) {
  r  <- rank(score)
  n1 <- sum(actual == 1); n0 <- sum(actual == 0)
  (sum(r[actual == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
c(year_model = auc(test$is_year, test$p_year),
  id_model   = auc(test$is_id,   test$p_id))
```

An AUC near 0.95 says the identifier model's scores are informative --- it is the
0.5 rule that is throwing the information away. That is the signal that **changing
the threshold will help**.

## Improving the lopsided model by changing the threshold

The cutoff is a choice, not a property of the model. Lowering it turns more
columns into "yes" calls: sensitivity goes up, specificity (and usually precision)
go down. Let's see the whole trade-off by sweeping the cutoff from 0.01 to 0.99.

**Important:** the threshold is a tuning parameter, so we pick it using the
*training* data and only then check it on the test data. Choosing it by peeking at
the test set would make the test-set numbers optimistic.

```{r sweep}
train$p_id <- predict(m_id, newdata = train, type = "response")

sweep_thresholds <- function(actual, prob, cutoffs = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) {
  out <- t(sapply(cutoffs, function(k) metrics(actual, as.integer(prob > k))))
  data.frame(cutoff = cutoffs, out)
}
sw <- sweep_thresholds(train$is_id, train$p_id)
round(sw[round(sw$cutoff, 2) %in% c(0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7),
         c("cutoff", "TP", "FP", "FN", "sensitivity", "specificity",
           "precision", "F1", "balanced_accuracy")], 3)
```

```{r sweep-plot}
plot(sw$cutoff, sw$sensitivity, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     ylim = c(0, 1.12), xlab = "probability cutoff", ylab = "metric (training data)",
     main = "Identifier model: metrics across cutoffs")
lines(sw$cutoff, sw$specificity, lwd = 2, col = "gray40")
lines(sw$cutoff, sw$precision,   lwd = 2, col = "darkorange")
lines(sw$cutoff, sw$F1,          lwd = 2, col = "forestgreen", lty = 2)
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 3)
legend("top", bty = "n", lwd = 2, ncol = 4, cex = 0.85,
       col = c("steelblue", "gray40", "darkorange", "forestgreen"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
       legend = c("sensitivity", "specificity", "precision", "F1"))
```

Specificity barely moves across the whole range --- there are so many
non-identifiers, and most score near zero, that even a low cutoff flags only a
handful of them. Sensitivity, on the other hand, climbs steeply as the cutoff
drops. Somewhere around 0.1--0.3 the model catches far more identifiers at a small
cost in precision.

### The ROC curve

The ROC curve plots the same sweep as sensitivity against the false-positive rate
(1 − specificity). Each cutoff is one point; the 0.5 cutoff is marked.

```{r roc, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
roc <- sweep_thresholds(train$is_id, train$p_id, cutoffs = seq(0, 1, by = 0.005))
plot(1 - roc$specificity, roc$sensitivity, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "false positive rate (1 - specificity)", ylab = "sensitivity",
     main = "ROC curve, identifier model (training)")
abline(0, 1, lty = 3, col = "gray50")
at50 <- which.min(abs(roc$cutoff - 0.5))
points(1 - roc$specificity[at50], roc$sensitivity[at50], pch = 19, col = "firebrick")
text(1 - roc$specificity[at50], roc$sensitivity[at50], "cutoff 0.5",
     pos = 4, col = "firebrick")
```

The 0.5 point sits low on the curve, where it is hugging the left axis. The curve
rises steeply to its right: big gains in sensitivity are available for very little
movement in the false-positive rate.

### Two neutral ways to pick a cutoff

When you have no cost information, two common rules are:

- **Maximize F1** --- balances precision and recall; ignores true negatives, so it
  is a good default for rare-positive problems.
- **Maximize Youden's J** = sensitivity + specificity − 1, the point on the ROC
  curve farthest above the diagonal (equivalently, maximum balanced accuracy).

```{r neutral-cutoffs}
k_f1    <- sw$cutoff[which.max(sw$F1)]
k_youden <- sw$cutoff[which.max(sw$sensitivity + sw$specificity - 1)]
c(max_F1 = k_f1, max_Youden = k_youden)
```

Youden's J treats a missed identifier and a false alarm as equally bad *in rate
terms*, and because negatives vastly outnumber positives it tends to push the
cutoff very low and accept many false positives. F1 is usually more conservative.
Neither is "right" --- each encodes an implicit judgement about costs. The better
approach is to make that judgement explicit.

## Choosing a threshold when errors have different costs

In practice the two kinds of mistakes rarely cost the same. For the identifier
model:

- A **false negative** --- an ID column treated as an ordinary number --- is
  expensive. Downstream code may average it, round it, or strip its leading zeros
  (`00721` → `721`), silently corrupting a key that other tables join on.
- A **false positive** --- an ordinary column flagged as a possible ID --- is
  cheap. A person glances at it and clears the flag.

Suppose a missed ID costs **5 units** (say, 5 minutes of debugging, amortized) and a
false alarm costs **1 unit** (a 1-minute review). The total cost of a cutoff is

$$\text{cost}(k) = c_{FN}\cdot FN(k) + c_{FP}\cdot FP(k),$$

and we choose the $k$ that minimizes it.

```{r cost-sweep}
c_fn <- 5
c_fp <- 1
sw$cost <- c_fn * sw$FN + c_fp * sw$FP
k_cost  <- sw$cutoff[which.min(sw$cost)]
k_cost
```

```{r cost-plot}
plot(sw$cutoff, sw$cost, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "purple",
     xlab = "probability cutoff", ylab = "total cost (training data)",
     main = sprintf("Cost of errors: FN = %d, FP = %d", c_fn, c_fp))
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 3)
abline(v = k_cost, lty = 2, col = "purple")
text(k_cost, max(sw$cost) * 0.9, sprintf("min-cost cutoff = %.2f", k_cost),
     pos = 4, col = "purple")
```

### A shortcut from decision theory

If the model's probabilities are well calibrated, the cost-minimizing rule has a
closed form. Call a column positive when the *expected* cost of saying "no" exceeds
the expected cost of saying "yes":

$$p \cdot c_{FN} > (1 - p)\cdot c_{FP}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.$$

With $c_{FN} = 5$ and $c_{FP} = 1$ the theoretical cutoff is
$1/6 \approx `r f3(1 / 6)`$. The default 0.5 cutoff is just the special case
$c_{FP} = c_{FN}$: it is optimal **only when both errors cost the same**.

```{r cost-theory}
c(theory = c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn), empirical = k_cost)
```

Here the two disagree: the formula says `r f2(c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn))`, the sweep
says `r f2(k_cost)`. The formula is only as good as the probabilities fed into it,
and this model's probabilities are **not perfectly calibrated**. You can check
calibration directly by binning the predictions and comparing the average
predicted probability with the observed share of identifiers in each bin:

```{r calibration}
bins <- cut(train$p_id, c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1),
            include.lowest = TRUE)
round(cbind(columns        = table(bins),
            mean_predicted = tapply(train$p_id,  bins, mean),
            observed_rate  = tapply(train$is_id, bins, mean)), 3)
```

In the low-to-middle bins the model **over**-states the chance of an identifier
(in the 0.2--0.3 bin it predicts about 25%, but only about 11% are IDs), and in
the top bin it **under**-states it. Over-stated low scores mean a cutoff of
`r f2(c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn))` lets in more false positives than the formula
expects, so the real optimum sits higher. The difference matters: on the training
data the total cost is
`r with(sw[which.min(abs(sw$cutoff - 0.5)), ], c_fn * FN + c_fp * FP)` at the
default 0.5,
`r with(sw[which.min(abs(sw$cutoff - c_fp / (c_fp + c_fn))), ], c_fn * FN + c_fp * FP)`
at the theoretical cutoff (barely an improvement, because the extra false positives
eat up most of the gain), and `r min(sw$cost)` at the empirical one.

The empirical sweep counts each kind of error at each cutoff, so it doesn't depend
on the probabilities being calibrated. **When the formula and the sweep disagree,
trust the sweep**, and treat the gap as a sign that the model's probabilities
shouldn't be read literally. (With very few positives the sweep can be noisy too;
cross-validation or a separate validation set gives a steadier estimate.)

### Check the chosen cutoff on the test set

Now --- and only now --- we apply the cutoffs chosen on training data to the
held-out test set and compare them with the default.

```{r compare-test}
cutoffs <- c(default_0.5 = 0.5, max_F1 = k_f1,
             min_cost_5to1 = k_cost, max_Youden = k_youden)
cmp <- t(sapply(cutoffs, function(k) {
  m <- metrics(test$is_id, as.integer(test$p_id > k))
  c(cutoff = k, m[c("TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "accuracy", "sensitivity",
                    "specificity", "precision", "F1", "balanced_accuracy")],
    cost = unname(c_fn * m["FN"] + c_fp * m["FP"]))
}))
round(cmp, 3)
```

```{r cmp-numbers, include = FALSE}
d50 <- cmp["default_0.5", ]; dc <- cmp["min_cost_5to1", ]
```

The confusion matrix at the cost-minimizing cutoff:

```{r cm-id-tuned}
confusion(test$is_id, as.integer(test$p_id > k_cost))
```

Reading the comparison:

- Moving the cutoff from 0.5 to `r f2(k_cost)` raises **sensitivity from
  `r f2(d50["sensitivity"])` to `r f2(dc["sensitivity"])`** --- the
  model now catches `r dc["TP"]` identifiers instead of `r d50["TP"]`.
- The price is `r dc["FP"] - d50["FP"]` additional false positive(s);
  **specificity stays at `r f3(dc["specificity"])`** and precision moves from
  `r f2(d50["precision"])` to `r f2(dc["precision"])`.
- **Total cost falls from `r d50["cost"]` to `r dc["cost"]`** on the test set,
  and balanced accuracy rises from `r f2(d50["balanced_accuracy"])` to
  `r f2(dc["balanced_accuracy"])`.
- Accuracy barely changes. Had we judged the models by accuracy alone we would
  never have noticed either the problem or the fix.

### How the best cutoff depends on the cost ratio

The cutoff is a policy decision. Different cost ratios lead to different cutoffs
and different error mixes:

```{r cost-ratios}
ratios <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20)       # cost of a FN relative to a FP
pol <- t(sapply(ratios, function(r) {
  k <- sw$cutoff[which.min(r * sw$FN + 1 * sw$FP)]   # chosen on training data
  m <- metrics(test$is_id, as.integer(test$p_id > k)) # evaluated on test data
  c(FN_cost = r, theory = 1 / (1 + r), chosen = k,
    m[c("TP", "FP", "FN", "sensitivity", "precision")])
}))
round(pol, 3)
```

As missing an identifier becomes more expensive, the cutoff falls, sensitivity
rises, and we accept more false alarms to get there. Note that even at a 1:1 ratio
the best cutoff on the training data is below 0.5 --- another symptom of the
calibration gap --- while at high ratios (10:1, 20:1) the chosen cutoff tracks the
theoretical one closely.

### Does the year model need the same treatment?

Not much. Its scores already separate the classes cleanly at 0.5, so there are few
borderline cases for a new cutoff to rescue:

```{r year-cost}
train$p_year <- predict(m_year, newdata = train, type = "response")
sw_y <- sweep_thresholds(train$is_year, train$p_year)
k_year <- sw_y$cutoff[which.min(c_fn * sw_y$FN + c_fp * sw_y$FP)]
rbind(default_0.5 = metrics(test$is_year, as.integer(test$p_year > 0.5)),
      min_cost    = metrics(test$is_year, as.integer(test$p_year > k_year)))[
  , c("TP", "FP", "FN", "sensitivity", "precision", "F1")]
```

Threshold tuning helps most when the model **ranks well but is mis-cut** --- high
AUC with lopsided sensitivity and specificity. It cannot help a model whose scores
don't separate the classes; that model needs better features, not a new cutoff.

## Summary

- `glm(y ~ ..., family = binomial)` fits a logistic regression;
  `predict(..., type = "response")` returns probabilities; a cutoff turns them into
  classes.
- The **confusion matrix** is the source of every metric. Report several:
  sensitivity and precision for the positive class, specificity for the negative
  class, and F1 or balanced accuracy as a summary.
- For a **rare outcome, accuracy is nearly useless**: compare it with the
  no-information rate.
- A model with **high AUC but low sensitivity** at 0.5 is ranking well and cutting
  badly. Lower the cutoff.
- **Choose the cutoff on training (or validation) data**, never on the test set.
- When the two errors cost different amounts, minimize
  $c_{FN}\cdot FN + c_{FP}\cdot FP$. With calibrated probabilities the answer is
  $p > c_{FP} / (c_{FP} + c_{FN})$; 0.5 is the special case of equal costs.

### Exercises

1. Refit the identifier model without `dig_entropy`. How much do AUC and the
   min-cost sensitivity fall?
2. Add `is_fixed_width` to the year model. Do any of the missed years get caught?
3. Suppose a false positive is the expensive error (every flagged column triggers
   a costly manual audit), with $c_{FP} = 5$ and $c_{FN} = 1$. Where does the
   cutoff move, and what happens to precision?
